title: Takayasu Arteritis with Neurological Manifestations: Clinical and Neurovascular Imaging Characteristics.
authors: Amira A Shahin; Hania S Zayed; Shereen Fathi; Nora Y Elsaid
abstract:
Takayasu arteritis (TA) is a large vessel vasculitis that may be accompanied by neurologi cal involvement in 57%-80% of the patients. The aim of this work is to describe the clinical and neuro vascular imaging abnormalities in TA patients with neurological manifestations.
Thirty-nine TA patients with neurological manifestations and available brain magnetic reso nance imaging (MRI), MR angiography (MRA), and MR venography of the intracranial and cervical vessels were studied. Patients with thrombophilia or hyperlipidemia were excluded.
The mean age at TA diagnosis was 30.56 ± 8.74 years, and 33 (84.62%) of the patients were women. The most frequent neurological manifestations included headaches (64.1%), syncope (12.8%), and visual loss (10.26%). According to the angiographic classification, 37 (94.9%) of the patients had involvement of branches from the aortic arch (Type I), and only 2 (5.1%) had diffuse aortic involve ment (Type V). Steno-occlusive lesions of the medium-sized intracranial arteries were observed in 11 (28.21%) of the patients. Features suggestive of small vessel disease were found among 16 (41%); 13 had abnormal MRI findings and 3 other patients had normal MRI and increased collateral circulation on MRA without associated intracranial arterial stenosis. Opening of the collateral circulation was seen in 14 (35.9%) patients. Venous involvement (affecting the cerebral venous sinuses and jugular veins) was found in 12 (30.77%) patients.
Patients with TA and neurological manifestations exhibit a spectrum of extracranial and intracranial vascular abnormalities including large, medium, and small blood vessels, as well as the cerebral venous sinuses and jugular veins.   Cite this article as: Shahin AA, Zayed HS, Fathi S, Elsaid NY. Takayasu arteritis with neurological manifestations: clinical and neurovascular imaging characteristics. Eur J Rheumatol. 2025, 12(4), 0003, doi:10.5152/eurjrheum.2025.25003.

title: Bentall procedure in the small aortoannular complex: impact of the implantation plane on prosthesis upsizing and early outcomes-a retrospective cohort study.
authors: Ünsal Vural; Yiğit Köse; Halil Emre Özlü
abstract:
Proximal conduit geometry may affect prosthesis accommodation during Bentall surgery for severe aortic stenosis and a small aortoannular complex. We compared subannular-supported supra-annular conduit implantation (SSSC) with supra-annular-supported annular conduit implantation (SSAC) for nominal size gain and early outcomes.
This retrospective cohort included 402 adults undergoing mechanical Bentall surgery between January 2020 and April 2026 (SSSC, n = 164; SSAC, n = 238). After leaflet excision and annular debridement, the largest manufacturer sizer accepted before suture/pledget placement defined the presuture expected size; repeat sizing after interrupted pledgeted sutures guided final conduit selection. The primary endpoint was implanted nominal size minus presuture expected size. Preoperative computed tomography characterized anatomy without conversion to nominal size, and body-size variables were recalculated from corrected measurements. Routine transthoracic echocardiography on postoperative days 5-7 measured continuity-equation effective orifice area (EOA), indexed EOA (EOAi), prosthesis-patient mismatch (PPM), and Doppler gradients. The 24-patient narrow sinotubular junction-proximal ascending aorta subgroup was analyzed separately.
SSSC yielded larger implanted size (23.4 ± 1.4 vs. 22.0 ± 1.1 mm) and nominal size gain (3.3 ± 1.1 vs. 1.9 ± 0.9 mm; both p < 0.001). After adjustment for corrected body size, baseline anatomy, and patient characteristics, SSSC remained associated with 0.99 mm greater gain (95% CI, 0.78-1.19; p < 0.001), higher EOA (+ 0.108 cm²) and EOAi (+ 0.063 cm²/m²), and lower odds of moderate PPM (adjusted odds ratio, 0.15; all p < 0.001). The adjusted mean-gradient difference was nonsignificant and the peak-gradient difference small. Permanent pacemaker implantation was more frequent after SSSC (7.9% vs. 2.1%; p = 0.007), whereas mortality was similar.
SSSC was associated with approximately 1 mm greater adjusted nominal size gain and more favorable early prosthesis-patient hemodynamics than SSAC, without demonstrated overall clinical superiority. The higher pacemaker rate warrants longer-term evaluation.
Not applicable. This retrospective observational study did not prospectively assign participants to a health-related intervention.

title: Afterload-Adjusted Strain Refines Risk Stratification in Aortic Stenosis With Varying Degrees of Aortic Regurgitation.
authors: Jonghee Sun; Jiesuck Park; Hyoung-Won Cho; Minjung Bak; Hong-Mi Choi; In-Chang Hwang; Yeonyee E Yoon; Goo-Yeong Cho
abstract:
In aortic stenosis (AS), concomitant aortic regurgitation (AR) may cause heterogeneous left ventricular (LV) remodeling and myocardial responses beyond valve-centric assessment. We evaluated LV geometry and myocardial deformation relative to systolic pressure load in patients with AS across varying AR severity.
We analyzed 950 patients with moderate or greater AS categorized as no, mild AR, or moderate or greater AR. LV geometry was assessed using left ventricular mass index (LVMI) and relative wall thickness (RWT). Afterload-adjusted strain (AAS) was calculated as absolute LV global longitudinal strain multiplied by estimated LV systolic pressure. The primary outcome was all-cause death or heart failure hospitalization.
During a median 3.5-year follow-up, 122 primary events occurred. Increasing AR severity was associated with LV dilation, increased LVMI, and reduced RWT, whereas AAS remained similar across AR categories. LV geometric measures were not independently associated with the primary outcome. Lower AAS was independently associated with the primary outcome (adjusted hazard ratio [HR], 1.33 per 500-unit decrease; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.12-1.58; p=0.001; adjusted HR, 1.41 per 1-standard deviation decrease, 95% CI, 1.14-1.73; p=0.001). AAS provided incremental prognostic value beyond clinical and LV geometric variables, increasing 1-year area under the curve from 0.762 to 0.788 (p<0.001).
Among patients with moderate or greater AS, increasing AR severity was associated with progressive LV remodeling, whereas lower AAS was independently associated with adverse outcomes. Relating myocardial deformation to systolic pressure load may refine risk stratification beyond clinical and LV geometric measures.

title: Operative management and outcomes of symptomatic carotid near occlusions stenosis.
authors: Aleksandar Dimov; Alexandru Toma; Joseph Kletzer; Wolf-Dirk Niesen; Maximilian Kreibich; Yasin El Mokhtari; Martin Czerny; Stoyan Kondov
abstract:
To present the outcomes of carotid endarterectomy (CEA) in patients with symptomatic carotid near-occlusion (CNO) and to compare these outcomes with those of patients with symptomatic non-CNO carotid stenosis.
This retrospective analysis included patients who underwent CEA of the internal carotid artery between January 2011 and December 2025. Outcomes in patients with symptomatic CNO were compared with those in patients with symptomatic non-CNO using propensity score matching on sex, age, amaurosis fugax, hyperlipidaemia, emergency status, and shunt as matching covariates. The primary endpoint was perioperative stroke, defined as a stroke occurring within 30 days after surgery. Secondary endpoints were cranial nerve injury, cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome, myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery, surgical revision, bleeding complications, reintubation, and in-hospital mortality.
In the unmatched cohort, 1,321 patients underwent carotid endarterectomy (CEA), of whom 85 (6.4%) presented with symptomatic CNO. After propensity score matching (2:1), 255 patients were analysed, comprising 85 with symptomatic CNO and 170 matched controls with symptomatic non-CNO stenosis. Baseline and operative characteristics were well balanced. The perioperative stroke rate was similar between patients with symptomatic CNO and those with symptomatic non-CNO stenosis (1.2% vs. 2.4%). No significant differences were observed in myocardial injury (2.4% vs. 2.4%, p>0.9), cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome (13% vs. 14%, p>0.9), cranial nerve injury (5.9% vs. 4.1%, p=0.5), surgical revision (7.1% vs. 5.9%, p=0.7), or postoperative bleeding (5.9% vs. 5.3%, p>0.9).
Carotid endarterectomy using the eversion technique appears feasible and can be performed with an acceptable perioperative complication rate in selected patients with symptomatic carotid near-occlusion. Although no statistically significant differences in perioperative outcomes were observed compared with patients undergoing CEA for conventional symptomatic carotid stenosis, the limited sample size and low event rates preclude conclusions about equivalence. Further studies with larger cohorts and long-term neurological follow-up are warranted to establish the clinical benefit of surgical revascularisation in this patient population.

title: Branched Endovascular Aortic Repair as a Salvage Strategy after Failed Chimney Endovascular Aortic Repair: An International Multicentre Cohort.
authors: Gioele Simonte; Marco Virgilio Usai; Giacomo Isernia; Gianbattista Parlani; Tal M Hörer; Enrico Gallitto; Nikolaos Tsilimparis; Benedikt Reutersberg; Nuno V Dias; Martin J Austermann; Mario D'Oria; BEVARinCHEVAR collaborative group
journal: European journal of vascular and endovascular surgery : the official journal of the European Society for Vascular Surgery
abstract:
Chimney endovascular aortic repair (chEVAR) failures, often manifesting as late type Ia endoleaks or sac expansion, present a formidable surgical challenge. Due to the variable upward orientation of pre-existing chimney stents, fenestrated solutions are frequently technically precluded. This study aimed to evaluate the outcomes of branched endovascular aortic repair (BEVAR) as a salvage strategy for late chEVAR failure within a multicentre international cohort.
A retrospective analysis was conducted on 29 consecutive patients (median age 81.0 years, interquartile range [IQR] 66.0, 83.0) treated across 13 European centres (2013 - 2025) for failed chEVAR using branched endografts. The primary endpoints were technical success, thirty day clinical success, and procedure related complications. Secondary endpoints included overall survival, freedom from re-intervention, and target visceral vessel (TVV) patency.
The median interval from index chEVAR to BEVAR re-intervention was 48.5 months (IQR 30.0, 80.8). Acute urgent or emergent procedures accounted for 17% of cases (n = 5), while 31% (n = 9) underwent expedited repair for large aneurysms. Off the shelf devices were utilised in 41% of cases. A total of 106 TVVs were incorporated through branches, with a mean of 3.7 vessels per patient. Technical success was achieved in 97% (28 of 29). There was no peri-operative mortality or open surgical conversion. Significant complications included two cases (7%) of severe spinal cord ischaemia. The thirty day clinical success rate was 90%. At a median follow up of 19 months (IQR 9, 40), the Kaplan-Meier estimate for overall survival was 92% at 1 year. TVV patency was 100%, with only one renal artery re-intervention for in stent re-stenosis. Freedom from branch related re-intervention was 96% at 1 year.
Salvage of failed chEVAR using branched endografts is technically demanding but yields excellent early results. In experienced centres, BEVAR appears feasible and offers one potential salvage option in selected patients with suitable anatomy, particularly when an off the shelf solution is required.

title: Predictors and Mid-Term Outcomes of Vascular Complications After Large-Bore Plug-Based Access-Site Closure in Patients Undergoing Transfemoral TAVI: A CHOICE-CLOSURE Substudy.
authors: Anna Roeßler; Oliver Dumpies; Philipp Hartung; Johannes Rotta Detto Loria; Ines Richter; Niklas Lankisch; Hans-Josef Feistritzer; Nicolas Majunke; Philipp Kiefer; Thilo Noack; Steffen Desch; Holger Thiele; Mohamed Abdel-Wahab
journal: Catheterization and cardiovascular interventions : official journal of the Society for Cardiac Angiography & Interventions
abstract:
The plug-based MANTA (Teleflex, Pennsylvania, USA) vascular closure device (VCD) is an alternative to suture-based VCDs for large-bore arterial closure after transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI), but has been associated with higher rates of vascular complications. Predictors and outcomes of these complications are not well-analyzed, especially regarding the self-resorbing characteristics of the MANTA VCD.
To identify predictors of access-site related vascular complications following transfemoral TAVI with the MANTA VCD, and to assess mid-term outcomes and late-onset events (after 30 days) in affected patients.
This prospective substudy of the CHOICE-CLOSURE trial included all patients randomized to vascular closure with the MANTA VCD at the Leipzig Heart Center. Patients with vascular complications, defined according to the Valve Academic Research Consortium (VARC)-2 criteria, underwent additional clinical and ultrasound follow-up, at least 6 months after the index procedure. Predictors of vascular complications were assessed through multivariable analysis.
Of 237 patients treated with the MANTA VCD, 46 (19.4%) had an access-site related vascular complication. Pre-procedural dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) was the only independent predictor in multivariable analysis (Odds ratio 4.27, 95% confidence interval 1.58-11.59, p = 0.004). At a mean follow-up of 13.5 months, no new vascular complications occurred. Patients with an over-stented MANTA VCD (n = 5) had no in-stent stenosis, and stent diameters further expanded by 12.5% to 20.0%.
Pre-procedural DAPT independently predicted vascular complications after TAVI in MANTA patients. Patients with vascular complications had no further access-site late-onset events, and endovascular stenting of a MANTA VCD appeared safe.

title: Bioprosthetic valve performance of transcatheter aortic valves.
authors: Stephan Windecker; Ole De Backer; Philippe Pibarot; Victoria Delgado; Daijiro Tomii
journal: EuroIntervention : journal of EuroPCR in collaboration with the Working Group on Interventional Cardiology of the European Society of Cardiology
abstract: Transcatheter aortic valve implantation is used increasingly in younger patients with longer life expectancy, necessitating long-term effectiveness. Randomised clinical trials have demonstrated comparable or superior haemodynamic performance of transcatheter heart valves (THVs) to surgical aortic valve replacement over midterm follow-up. Within a lifetime management framework, haemodynamic performance and durability of THVs are central considerations in patients undergoing aortic valve replacement for severe aortic stenosis. This review provides an overview of THV design and function along with contemporary clinical evidence, with a focus on current haemodynamic assessment considerations, challenges in cross-platform interpretation of valve performance, and limitations of randomised comparative evidence, as well as future directions in the evaluation of THV performance.

title: Three-year outcomes of balloon-expandable valve-in-valve aortic valve implantation for failed transcatheter versus surgical valves.
authors: Hidemasa Shitan; Vivek Patel; Kazuki Suruga; Yuchao Guo; Takashi Nagasaka; Melanie Ng; Elijah Buss; Nikitaa Gandhi; Daniel Ng; Dhairya Patel; Jaideep Menda; Aakriti Gupta; Tarun Chakravarty; Wen Cheng; Yuito Okada; Hasan Jilaihawi; Mamoo Nakamura; Raj R Makkar
journal: EuroIntervention : journal of EuroPCR in collaboration with the Working Group on Interventional Cardiology of the European Society of Cardiology
abstract:
Clinical outcomes after transcatheter aortic valve (TAV)-in-TAV compared with TAV-in-surgical aortic valve (SAV) implantation for failed bioprosthetic valves have been limited to short-term outcomes.
This study compared midterm outcomes between patients undergoing TAV-in-TAV and those undergoing TAV-in-SAV.
From June 2015 to June 2024, 543 consecutive patients undergoing valve-in-valve (ViV) transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) were identified at our centre. After exclusion of ineligible patients, 109 patients undergoing TAV-in-TAV and 349 undergoing TAV-in-SAV were included. Following propensity score matching, 214 patients (107 per group) were analysed.
Three-year all-cause mortality did not differ between the TAV-in-TAV and TAV-in-SAV groups (hazard ratio 1.06, 95% confidence interval: 0.56-1.98; p=0.867). Similarly, no significant differences were detected in secondary outcomes. Over 3 years, the aortic valve mean pressure gradient was consistently lower and the aortic valve area was consistently larger in the TAV-in-TAV group compared with the TAV-in-SAV group. Concomitant percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and coronary obstruction were more frequent in the TAV-in-SAV group than in the TAV-in-TAV group (22.4% vs 8.4%; p=0.006; 10.3% vs 0.9%; p=0.018, respectively). Post-ViV-TAVI computed tomography analysis showed that the waist level was the least expanded segment in both groups. However, expansion at this level was significantly greater in the TAV-in-TAV group than in the TAV-in-SAV group.
There was no significant difference in 3-year mortality between the TAV-in-TAV and TAV-in-SAV groups. However, TAV-in-SAV was associated with higher rates of concomitant PCI and coronary obstruction, as well as lower valve expansion.

title: Outcomes of Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement for Aortic Regurgitation in LVAD Patients: The JENA-VAD Study.
authors: Ravi Ramana; Nir Uriel; Pradeep Yadav; Lowell Satler; Lauren S Ranard; Toby Rogers; Ron Waksman; Itsik Ben-Dor; Raj Makkar; Aakriti Gupta; Tiberio Frisoli; Pedro Villablanca; Srinivasa Potluri; Katherine Harrington; Brian Whisenant; Alan Zajarias; Tsuyoshi Kaneko; James Stewart; David Daniels; Adam Greenbaum; Vasilis Babaliaros; Stan Chetcuti; Gorav Ailawadi; Harsh Golwala; Mark Russo; Sachin Goel; Marvin D Atkins; Matthew Summers; Clinton Kemp; Konstantinos Voudris; Axel Unbehaun; Taya Ramana; Michael Chuang; Antone J Tatooles; Martin Fahy; Duane S Pinto; Vinod H Thourani; Torsten P Vahl; Martin B Leon; Gabriel Sayer; JENA-VAD Investigators
journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
abstract:
Aortic regurgitation (AR) during left ventricular assist device (LVAD) support causes recurrent heart failure. Surgery is high risk and stenosis-designed valves anchor poorly in noncalcified anatomy.
The goal of this study was to evaluate early outcomes of the AR-specific Trilogy transcatheter heart valve for LVAD-associated AR.
JENA-VAD is a prospective, multicenter, single-arm investigational device exemption study. An independent committee adjudicated endpoints using VARC-3 (Valve Academic Research Consortium-3) definitions. The primary efficacy endpoint was the VARC-3 device success composite adapted for LVAD support, and the primary safety endpoint was the VARC-3 early safety composite.
Fifty patients were treated (mean age 69.2 years; 40% female). Median follow-up was 105 days (range 27 to 577 days). Technical and device success were 96.0% (95% CI: 86.3-99.5). Freedom from any component event of the VARC-3 early safety composite was 90.0% (95% CI: 78.2-96.7). At 30 days, 7 VARC-3 safety events occurred in 5 patients: type 2 to 4 bleeding (n = 2), major vascular complications (n = 2), device-related peripheral interventions (n = 2), and new pacemaker (1 of 7 without prior pacing; 14.3%). There were no strokes or myocardial infarctions. Two transient ischemic attacks occurred in patients without valve abnormalities. Beyond 30 days, cardiovascular death occurred in 1 patient (day 86). Follow-up computed tomography (CT) imaging or transesophageal echocardiography was obtained in 12 patients, and 11 (including 3 within 30 days) had leaflet thickening or thrombosis, including all patients who underwent CT. The remaining 38 patients did not have postprocedure imaging. Two of these events were symptomatic: valve thrombosis and a transient ischemic attack (day 116), and prosthetic AR that required valve-in-valve implantation (day 146) and subsequent heart transplantation. In exploratory analyses, NYHA functional class at 30 days was I or II in 72.3% (34 of 47) and Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire overall summary score rose 11.5 ± 21.5 points (n = 44).
Transcatheter valve replacement using a dedicated system in LVAD patients was feasible with high technical and device success and without early death, stroke, or moderate or severe residual AR. Leaflet thickening or thrombosis, detected on clinically indicated CT imaging, occurred in 22%, representing a lower bound. Follow-up is ongoing to inform longer-term safety and effectiveness. (Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement Using the JenaValve Trilogy Heart Valve System for Clinically Significant Aortic Regurgitation in Patients With Left Ventricular Assist Devices [LVAD]; NCT06594705).

title: Valve Embolisation During Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation (TAVI): Clinical Outcomes and CT-Derived Anatomical Characteristics.
authors: Dominic Dalip; Amerjeet Banning; Raj Rajendra
abstract: Background Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has transformed the management of severe aortic stenosis, offering an effective alternative for elderly patients and those at high surgical risk who are not ideal candidates for open-heart surgery. Of late, there is an expansion into intermediate- and low-risk populations as well. Transcatheter valve embolisation or migration (TVEM) is a rare but potentially fatal complication. Predictors of TVEM are incompletely understood, and there is a gap in evidence, looking specifically at the CT-derived anatomical characteristics of TVEM. Aim This study aimed to quantify the incidence of TVEM in a high-volume tertiary centre and characterise anatomical patterns in patients experiencing TVEM during TAVI. Methods This is a retrospective, single-centre study. Patients registered as having TVEM were identified using the local database from June 2014 to June 2024. Case notes of these patients were then studied to assess the management of TVEM and outcomes. For this cohort of patients, preprocedural CTs were analysed in detail, including annulus perimeter and area, qualitative leaflet calcification grading (moderate, severe, very severe), presence of annular/aorto-mitral curtain (AMC) calcification, and minimum sinus of Valsalva (SOV) diameter. Procedural data included initial embolised valve type and the bailout strategy. Results The incidence of TVEM was 0.51% with a 30-day mortality of 40% and average length of stay in hospital of 11.5 days, compared with the uncomplicated TAVI length of stay averaging 2.1 days. There was a periprocedural complication of stroke in 10% of patients (1 patient) and no vascular access site complication. Leaflet calcification was severe or very severe in 9/10 patients, with AMC calcification present in half. The mean minimum SOV diameter was 28.7 +/- 3.5 mm (23-34 mm), and several cases demonstrated markedly constrained aortic root anatomy. All embolised valves were self-expanding devices. In 4/10 cases, a balloon-expandable THV was used as the second device, while 6/10 were treated with another self-expanding THV. Conclusion Findings suggest that TVEM is a rare complication associated with substantial short-term mortality. Severe leaflet calcification, AMC calcification, and smaller SOV dimensions were frequently observed in this cohort, and all embolised valves were self-expanding. These findings are descriptive and hypothesis-generating; without a comparator group, their association with embolisation risk cannot be established. However, these anatomical findings warrant careful preprocedural assessment, while prospective comparative studies are needed to determine their association with TVEM risk.

title: Impact Benchmark: Peer-to-Peer Quality-Improvement Program to Optimize Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation Processes and Resources.
authors: Sandra B Lauck; James Velianou; Alexander Dick; Malek Kass; Jean-Eric Tarride; Maggie Yu; Amanda N Smith; Anita Asgar; Jessica Forcillo; Osama Elkhateeb; Jean-François Légaré; Cheryl Low; Jaffer Syed; Neil Pearce; Janine Eckstein; Neil Fam; Manu Prabhakar; Albert Chan; Derk Frank; David A Wood; Talal Al-Atassi
abstract:
Patient demand for transcatheter aortic valve implantation is growing, and competing demands on program capacity are barriers to timely access to care for patients with aortic stenosis.
We report on the retrospective evaluation of the Impact Benchmark program in Canada, a peer-to-peer multidisciplinary quality-improvement initiative to accelerate the adoption of evidence-based best practices. Centres self-reported indicators of pre-, peri-, and post-procedure practices 6 months before and after their participation, and in 2024.
Between 2019 and 2023, a total of 18 of the 31 Canadian cardiac programs (58.1%) participated in the program; 14 of 18 (77.7%) reported on their experience. Pre-procedure, the mean time from referral to procedure decreased by 13 days. The assessment pathway was streamlined from 3 to 2 pre-procedure visits in 6 centres, and 8 centres transitioned to a process of individualized decision to perform diagnostic coronary angiography, with 11 of 14 (78.6%) reporting this practice in 2024. Peri-procedure changes included the de-escalation of anaesthesia strategy in 7 programs; 3 of the 4 centres that routinely held an operating room on standby, and 5 of the 9 programs that had open-heart surgery equipment open or available ceased these practices. Overall, a 27.6% and 20.9% decrease occurred in the mean procedure and total room time, respectively. Post-procedure, 6 centres established new processes to avoid critical care, with 11 (78.6%) now reporting this established process; 10 centres implemented new early mobilization protocols. Clinical outcomes remained excellent.
Structured, peer-enabled benchmarking across the care continuum for transcatheter aortic valve implantation drives practice change and program performance improvement.

title: Severe Rheumatic Mitral Stenosis With Multivalvular Abnormalities in a British-Born Adult Without a Recognized History of Acute Rheumatic Fever.
authors: Adel Kenawi; Hatem Ali Abdelnasser; Nouralhuda Hamad; Marwa Ruziek; Ahmed Jaber
abstract: Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) has become uncommon in the United Kingdom, particularly among British-born adults without a recognized history of acute rheumatic fever (ARF). A 40-year-old British-born female with no previously diagnosed cardiac disease presented with a one-year history of progressive exertional dyspnoea. Chest radiography demonstrated cardiomegaly, and the N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide concentration was 1,800 pg/mL. Transthoracic echocardiography showed very severe mitral stenosis with characteristic rheumatic morphology, a mitral valve area of 0.33 cm² by planimetry, and a mean transmitral gradient of 16.6 mmHg. Associated findings included mild mitral regurgitation, tricuspid valve abnormalities with moderate-to-severe tricuspid regurgitation, and discordant aortic valve findings consistent with a low-flow, low-gradient pattern of aortic stenosis, an estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of approximately 105-110 mmHg, left ventricular systolic impairment, and impaired right ventricular longitudinal systolic function. Further history identified intermittent involuntary left-hand movements, arthralgia, and an annular abdominal eruption with central pallor. These features raised the possibility of previously unrecognized rheumatic manifestations but were insufficient to establish the diagnosis of ARF. Following transoesophageal echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, and multidisciplinary review, the patient underwent mitral and aortic valve replacement with tricuspid valve repair. This case highlights that advanced RHD can present without a documented history of ARF and emphasizes the importance of valve morphology, integrated haemodynamic assessment, and timely multidisciplinary management.

title: Fibrosis Without Macrocalcification: A Novel In Vitro Model to Study Aortic Valve Disease.
authors: Emma Le Nezet; Chloé Marqueze-Pouey; Katy Vaillancourt; Vanessa Couture; Nancy Côté; Marie-Annick Clavel
abstract:
The absence of medical treatment for fibrocalcific aortic valve stenosis (FCAVS), despite its high incidence in high-income countries, emphasizes the need to discover novel therapeutic targets. Given the sex-specific differences in fibrotic and calcific pathways in FCAVS, in vitro approaches capable of independently dissecting these 2 processes must be developed. In this project we aim to characterize a new medium able to induce fibrosis specifically in valvular interstitial cells (VICs).
Human VICs were isolated from 10 explanted tricuspid aortic valves (5 men and 5 women) and treated with fibrotic and fibrocalcific media for 0, 7, and 14 days.
As expected, the fibrotic medium increased fibrotic markers (elevated procollagen I, procollagen III, and matrix metalloproteinase-2 levels), whereas the fibrocalcific medium induced calcification (decreased total Ca2+ levels in supernatants and increased calcific nodules detected by Alizarin Red staining) associated with mild fibrosis, in both male and female VICs (elevated procollagen I and procollagen III levels) without major sex-specific differences.
This novel fibrotic medium allows for the independent analysis of fibrotic pathways, distinct from calcification ones, in male- and female-derived VICs. The minimal sex-specific differences within each media suggest that sex-specific differences in FCAVS may be driven more by the surrounding milieu than by intrinsic cellular sex. This medium may help improve our understanding of the pathophysiologic processes underlying FCAVS.

title: Severe Pannus Formation with Coronary Artery Obstruction after the Ozaki Procedure: A Case Report.
authors: Yuichiro Kitada; Daniel O'Connor; Koji Takeda
abstract: We report a case of severe pannus formation causing coronary artery obstruction after aortic valve neocuspidization (the Ozaki procedure). A 64-year-old woman who had undergone the Ozaki procedure for aortic stenosis presented with chest pain. She was diagnosed with obstruction of the right coronary artery ostium and moderate aortic regurgitation and stenosis. Redo aortic valve replacement and coronary artery bypass grafting were subsequently performed. Surgery revealed severe circumferential pannus on the aortic side of the neocusps, with obstruction of the right coronary artery ostium. The pannus and cusps were removed completely; after aortic annular enlargement, the aortic valve was replaced. The patient's postoperative course was uneventful. This is the first case report of coronary obstruction due to pannus formation after the Ozaki procedure.

title: Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation in the Presence of Aortic Coarctation: Current Evidence and Practical Approaches.
authors: Vilhelmas Bajoras; Artiomas Širvys; Gintarė Petraitytė; Ričardas Kundelis; Liudas Usoris; Giedrius Davidavičius; Sigitas Čėsna
journal: Catheterization and cardiovascular interventions : official journal of the Society for Cardiac Angiography & Interventions
abstract:
Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has become an established treatment for severe aortic stenosis across a wide spectrum of surgical risk. As TAVI is increasingly used in younger patients and in those with congenital valve disease, the coexistence of aortic stenosis and untreated coarctation of the aorta (CoA) is being encountered more frequently. However, evidence guiding the procedural strategy in this complex anatomical setting remains limited.
To systematically review the published literature on TAVI in adult patients with untreated or residual coarctation of the aorta, focusing on patient characteristics, procedural strategies, vascular access selection, management of coexisting CoA, and clinical outcomes.
A systematic literature search was performed in PubMed, Wiley Online Library, ScienceDirect, and the Cochrane Library to identify published reports describing TAVI in adult patients with angiographically confirmed native or residual severe CoA. Case reports and case series published between January 2013 and September 2025 were included. Studies involving repaired CoA without restenosis or surgical aortic valve replacement were excluded. Clinical characteristics, access routes, procedural strategies, and outcomes were analyzed.
Nine patients from published reports met the inclusion criteria. Hemodynamically significant CoA was present in five patients (55.6%). Bicuspid aortic valve anatomy was reported in six cases. Transcatheter access routes included transcarotid (44.4%), transfemoral (33.3%), transsubclavian (11.1%), and transaxillary (11.1%) approaches. A staged strategy with initial CoA stenting followed by TAVI was performed in two patients (22.2%), whereas seven patients (77.8%) underwent single-procedure management, including concomitant treatment of both lesions in two cases. Procedural success was achieved in all cases, although technical challenges related to valve delivery and stent expansion were occasionally encountered.
TAVI in patients with untreated or residual CoA is feasible and can be performed with high procedural success when individualized strategies are applied. Access selection and the timing of CoA intervention should be guided by anatomical characteristics and hemodynamic severity. Given the limited evidence base, careful preprocedural planning and a multidisciplinary approach are essential to optimize outcomes in this complex patient population.

title: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: Patient Selection, Referral Timing, and Advanced Therapy Options.
authors: Mohammed Abusafia; Shada Jadam; Susan Ospina; Milind Y Desai
abstract: In this review, we provide a detailed up-to-date summary of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). From the complex and diverse presentations to the individualized clinical profiles, we delve into the different aspects of HCM diagnosis, management, and follow up. We discuss imaging modalities and their indications as well as current guidelines for both pharmacological and surgical treatment options. We also review the data regarding emerging therapies.

title: Strategy for Exercise Restriction in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy.
authors: Hyun-Jung Lee
abstract: This article outlines the evolving evidence and guidelines surrounding exercise in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), challenging the traditional paradigm of universal restriction. It highlights that most patients with HCM can safely engage in physical activity (PA) and improve cardiovascular outcomes. Recent evidence demonstrates that vigorous PA improves functional capacity and does not increase adverse events in most low-risk HCM patients. Contemporary guidelines advocate for individualized exercise recommendations based on comprehensive risk stratification and shared decision-making. A clinical framework is proposed to support tailored exercise prescriptions and shared decision-making.
